title: Distributed Rate Limiter
problem: Design a distributed rate limiter that protects APIs at 1M+ RPS with per-user / per-IP / per-API quotas.
summary: A distributed token-bucket rate limiter enforced at the API gateway, backed by Redis with atomic Lua scripts to avoid race conditions across gateway replicas (the chapter's two concrete concurrency-fix options are Lua scripts and Redis sorted sets). The dominant design choice is token bucket in Redis (O(1) per check, supports bursts — used in production by Amazon and Stripe per the book) over alternatives like sliding-window log (accurate but O(N) memory), sliding-window counter (Cloudflare-style hybrid, approximate but smooth), fixed window (cheap but allows 2x burst at boundaries), or leaking bucket (fixed output rate, no burst allowance). Rules are authored as Lyft-style YAML (domain/descriptor/unit/requests_per_unit), persisted on disk, and pulled by background workers into an in-memory rules cache so gateway hot-path lookups are cache-local. When a request is denied the gateway returns HTTP 429 with `X-Ratelimit-Limit`, `X-Ratelimit-Remaining`, and `X-Ratelimit-Retry-After`; soft-limited requests can optionally be deferred to a queue for later processing instead of being dropped. Multi-DC deployments place the limiter at edge POPs and reconcile counters under an eventual-consistency model.

functional: Enforce quotas per API key, per user, per IP, and per endpoint with configurable limits
Allow controlled bursts (e.g. 100 requests within 1s even on a 60/min quota) via token bucket
Return HTTP 429 with X-Ratelimit-Limit, X-Ratelimit-Remaining, and X-Ratelimit-Retry-After headers
Hot-reload rules from a control plane without restarting gateway replicas
Optionally enqueue soft-limited requests to a throttled queue instead of outright rejecting
Support composite keys (tenant + endpoint + method) and hierarchical quotas
nonFunctional: Add no more than 1-3ms of latency per request at 1M RPS fleet-wide
Correct under concurrency: two gateway replicas must not both allow a request that would exceed the budget
Highly available: limiter outage must not take down the API - fail open or fail to local cache
Horizontally scalable: adding gateway replicas must not add write contention
Low memory footprint: bucket state under 100 bytes per active identity

assumptions: Total traffic: 1M RPS across the fleet
Default limit: 100 req/min per user, 10K req/min per service key
Rule updates: <100/minute globally (very low write QPS)
estimates: Redis ops: 1M RPS * 1 script call each ≈ 1M RPS (single Redis cluster with 10 shards handles this)
Rules cache size per limiter replica: ~5 MB in-memory, O(1) hashmap lookup per request
Config service reads: rules-worker on each gateway polls every 5s → 100 / 5 = 20 RPS — negligible
Gateway overhead added per request: 1–3ms (local rules lookup + Redis RTT + Lua exec)
Multi-DC (per book): replicate counter deltas under an eventual-consistency model — brief over-admission across regions is acceptable for almost all APIs

client.name: Client (3rd-party / internal)
client.summary: Any caller hitting the public or internal API.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Attach auth identity (API key, OAuth token) so the limiter can attribute
- Respect `Retry-After` header on 429 with exponential backoff

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: A well-behaved client backs off on 429. A badly-behaved one retries instantly and compounds the problem — the limiter has to survive both.

bottlenecks.title: Retry storm on 429 ignoring Retry-After
bottlenecks.trigger: Misbehaving client retries immediately after 429 instead of honoring X-Ratelimit-Retry-After; at 1M RPS fleet-wide, even 1% of clients retrying at 10x amplifies denied traffic to ~100K extra RPS hitting the limiter hot path.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis shard CPU spikes on a few hot identities, gateway 429 rate climbs toward 100% for offending keys, p99 on the Lua script creeps from ~2ms toward 10ms+ due to hot-slot contention.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Ship a standard SDK with mandatory exponential backoff + jitter (e.g., base=1s, cap=60s) that parses X-Ratelimit-Retry-After; for abusive 3rd-party keys, escalate to a longer ban bucket (deny at LB via IP/API-key deny-list) rather than paying the Redis round-trip.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when ratio of (429s returned to a single api_key) / (allowed requests) > 5x sustained for 1min, or when per-identity request rate exceeds quota by >3x (indicates client ignoring Retry-After).

bottlenecks.title: Missing or spoofable identity attribution
bottlenecks.trigger: Client omits API key / OAuth token or shares a key across many tenants; limiter falls back to IP-based bucket, but NAT'd mobile carriers or corporate egress collapse thousands of users behind one IP, exhausting a single 100 req/min bucket.
bottlenecks.symptom: Legitimate users see 429s they didn't cause; support tickets cluster around specific ISPs or enterprise customers; X-Ratelimit-Remaining hits 0 far faster than user activity would predict.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Require auth before the rate-limit middleware (chapter's pipeline order: auth → rate-limiter); for anonymous endpoints use a composite key (IP + User-Agent + session cookie) instead of raw IP; publish guidance that each tenant provision its own API key.
bottlenecks.detection: Track per-bucket unique-source-IP cardinality; flag any api_key bucket with >100 distinct IPs/min or any IP bucket serving >10 distinct User-Agents as a shared-identity hotspot.

bottlenecks.title: Client-side latency amplification from synchronous 429 handling
bottlenecks.trigger: Client treats 202 Accepted (soft-limit enqueue path) as success but then polls aggressively for result, or blocks the user thread on 429 backoff; with 1–3ms limiter overhead plus 10–50ms upstream, a naive client can turn one user action into 5–10 gateway hits.
bottlenecks.symptom: Gateway sees 5-10x request multiplier per user action during throttling; throttled queue depth grows even when true arrival rate is within quota; user-perceived latency balloons to seconds.
bottlenecks.mitigation: SDK should handle 202 via async callback/webhook (deadline header from throttled-queue design), not polling; for 429, apply circuit-breaker pattern on the client to stop issuing requests for the full Retry-After window.
bottlenecks.detection: Compare unique-user-action count (from upstream business metrics) vs gateway request count per api_key; alert when amplification ratio > 2x, or when throttled-queue depth grows while upstream success rate is flat.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client is drawn on this diagram In most system design diagrams the client is a passive box — but for a rate limiter, the client's behavior is *part of the system you're designing*. The whole point of returning `429` with `X-Ratelimit-Retry-After` headers is that a cooperating client reads those headers and backs off. If the client ignores them, the limiter still works — it just keeps spending Redis CPU saying "no" a million times a second. So the client is on the diagram because the contract between gateway and caller (auth identity in, Retry-After out) is a design decision, not an implementation detail. ## What goes wrong if you ignore the client A misbehaving SDK retries immediately on every 429. The user sees their app hang or error out; the operator sees a single API key producing a flat wall of 429s, one Redis shard pegged at 100% CPU because all that caller's traffic hashes to one slot, and p99 on the Lua script creeping from 2ms toward 10ms+ as that slot contends. The gateway and Redis both take the hit for a problem the client caused. ## The arithmetic The design assumes 1M RPS fleet-wide. If just 1% of clients ignore `Retry-After` and retry at 10× on denial, that's `1M × 1% × 10 = 100K extra RPS` of pure denied traffic hammering the limiter — 10% of total capacity burned rejecting the same callers repeatedly. ## Trade-off You're trusting clients to be well-behaved for the common case, and escalating abusers to an LB-level deny-list so you don't pay the Redis round-trip for known-bad keys.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Least-connections. No user affinity needed — rate limiter state lives in Redis, not in gateways.

sections.heading: TLS
sections.body: Terminates TLS; hands off plaintext to gateways inside the VPC.

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU exhaustion at 1M RPS
bottlenecks.trigger: All 1M RPS fleet-wide terminates TLS at the LB. A modern LB core handles ~10-20K TLS handshakes/sec; with short-lived client connections (mobile, serverless callers) handshake rate can approach 50-100K/sec, saturating CPU before raw throughput limits.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegs at 100%, TLS handshake latency climbs from <5ms to 50ms+, clients see connection timeouts or TLS_HANDSHAKE_FAILED errors before ever reaching the gateway; p99 end-to-end latency explodes even though gateway and Redis are healthy.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS session resumption (session tickets + session ID cache, 24h TTL), require HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to amortize handshakes across many requests, offload to dedicated TLS-terminating nodes (e.g., AWS NLB+ACM or HAProxy with QAT hardware accel), and set keepalive_timeout to 75s to reuse connections.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB CPU >70% sustained 1min, TLS handshakes/sec >30K per node, or session-resumption-hit-ratio <80% (indicates clients aren't reusing sessions).

bottlenecks.title: Least-connections imbalance during gateway replica churn
bottlenecks.trigger: With 100 gateway replicas at ~10K RPS each and least-connections routing, a newly added or recovered replica shows 0 in-flight connections and attracts a thundering herd — potentially 50-100K RPS in the first second before counters equalize, far exceeding its 3000-concurrency limit.
bottlenecks.symptom: Freshly-deployed gateway replicas immediately hit 100% CPU, return 5xx or timeouts, and get flapped out of the pool; deploys trigger brief error-rate spikes visible as sawtooth pattern correlated with rolling restart cadence.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use slow-start (e.g., Envoy/NGINX slow_start=60s) to ramp traffic to new replicas linearly, cap per-backend max connections at 2x average (≈100 connections given 50 in-flight steady-state), and prefer P2C (power-of-two-choices) over pure least-connections to smooth variance.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when any single gateway replica sees >3x the fleet-median RPS for >10s, or when 5xx rate from any backend exceeds 1% during a deploy window.

bottlenecks.title: Connection table exhaustion under retry storm
bottlenecks.trigger: LB is configured for 50K concurrent connections. At 1M RPS with 50ms average upstream latency, steady-state in-flight is ~50K — already at capacity. A client retry storm (per the client component's bottleneck analysis, ~100K extra RPS from misbehaving callers) pushes concurrent conns past the table limit.
bottlenecks.symptom: New client SYNs are dropped or RST'd at the LB, existing connections remain healthy but new users cannot connect; `netstat` shows SYN_RECV backlog full; monitoring shows LB accept rate plateau while offered load climbs.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Raise conntrack/connection-table to 200K with matching file-descriptor and ephemeral-port tuning; enable SYN cookies; push abusive API keys and IPs to an LB-level deny-list (ties into the client deny-list mitigation) so they never consume a connection slot; enforce per-source-IP connection caps (e.g., 1000/IP).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB concurrent_connections >80% of configured limit (40K of 50K), SYN-drop counter >0, or accept-queue overflow in kernel counters (`nstat ListenOverflows`).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the load balancer is here The rate limiter has to handle **1M+ RPS** across the fleet, and no single machine can do that. The design spreads work across **100 gateway replicas**, each handling roughly 10K RPS. But clients don't know those replicas exist — they hit one DNS name. The load balancer is the thing that turns "one public endpoint" into "100 interchangeable workers." It also terminates TLS once at the edge, so each gateway doesn't burn CPU on handshakes, and it hides replica churn (deploys, crashes, autoscaling) from callers. ## What happens without it Without an LB, you'd have to either pin every client to a specific gateway (brittle: one replica dies and a slice of your users go dark) or do DNS round-robin (no health checks, so dead replicas keep getting traffic for minutes until TTLs expire). Operators would see lopsided CPU — some gateways at 100%, others idle — and users behind the hot replicas would see 429s and timeouts that have nothing to do with their actual quota. The rate limiter's own Redis shards would look healthy while the gateway tier silently melts. ## The arithmetic At 1M RPS across 100 replicas, each gateway handles ~10K RPS. If the LB's distribution is off by even 2× on one replica, that node suddenly sees 20K RPS against its **3000 concurrency** budget — it'll queue, then drop. The LB's least-connections algorithm exists specifically to keep that variance tight. ## Trade-off You've added one more hop (0–2ms) and one more thing to operate, in exchange for horizontal scalability and graceful replica failure.

gw.name: API Gateway
gw.summary: Edge service that runs auth + rate-limit middleware before proxying — the book's preferred host for rate limiting in a microservices architecture.

sections.heading: Why the gateway (per book)
sections.body: Chapter 4's 'Where to put the rate limiter?' section argues the rate limiter belongs in a middleware layer in front of API servers rather than inside each API. In a microservices architecture this naturally collapses into the API gateway, which already terminates TLS and does auth / IP whitelisting. Implementing it here keeps application services free of cross-cutting boilerplate.

sections.heading: Pipeline
sections.body: `request → auth → rate-limiter → upstream → response`

sections.heading: 429 response (with headers)
sections.body:
On deny: return `HTTP 429 Too Many Requests` with the three response headers the chapter defines:
- `X-Ratelimit-Limit` — total allowed in window
- `X-Ratelimit-Remaining` — what's left
- `X-Ratelimit-Retry-After` — seconds until next slot opens
Clients use these to back off correctly instead of hammering.

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Stateless. 1M RPS / 100 replicas ≈ 10K RPS each at ~5ms → 50 concurrent in-flight per replica, well under any single-box limit.

lost: Heavier than Envoy for pure gateway use

bottlenecks.title: Concurrency cap exhausted under upstream latency spike
bottlenecks.trigger: Each gateway replica is configured with concurrency=3000 and handles ~10K RPS. Steady-state in-flight is ~10K RPS × 50ms upstream = 500 concurrent. If upstream p99 jumps from 50ms to 300ms (GC pause, DB lock, dependency slowdown), in-flight climbs to 10K × 0.3 = 3000 — exactly the replica's concurrency limit — and any further arrival is rejected or queued.
bottlenecks.symptom: Gateway replicas return 503 or connection resets, p99 latency climbs into seconds, LB marks replicas unhealthy and shifts load to survivors which then tip over in cascade; 429s from the limiter look normal but non-limited traffic also fails.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set an explicit per-replica in-flight budget (e.g., Envoy max_concurrent_requests=2500 with 20% headroom), enable adaptive concurrency (Envoy's gradient controller or Netflix concurrency-limits lib), and shed load with 503+Retry-After before hitting the hard cap. Size replica count so steady-state in-flight ≤ 30% of concurrency limit.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-replica in_flight_requests > 70% of concurrency (2100 of 3000) for 30s, or on upstream_latency_p99 > 2× baseline, or on any 503 from gateway (distinct from the expected 429s).

bottlenecks.title: Auth middleware latency dominates the request budget
bottlenecks.trigger: Pipeline is `auth → rate-limiter → upstream`. Gateway service time is budgeted at 3–10ms total, of which the rate-limiter itself uses 1–4ms and Redis RTT 1–3ms. Auth (JWT verify, OAuth introspection, or API-key DB lookup) can easily consume 5–20ms per request if it calls an external IdP or uncached key store — at 10K RPS per replica that's either saturating the IdP or adding 2-4× to gateway latency.
bottlenecks.symptom: Gateway p99 creeps from the modeled 10ms to 30–50ms even when Redis and upstream are healthy; CPU profiles show most time in TLS/JWT verify or waiting on introspection HTTP calls; throughput per replica drops below 10K RPS forcing autoscaler to add gateways unnecessarily.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache auth results locally (LRU keyed by token hash, TTL=60s, hit-rate target >95%); prefer stateless JWT verification with cached JWKS over remote introspection; pool connections to the IdP with circuit breakers; move expensive key-DB lookups behind the same rules-worker pattern used for rate-limit rules.
bottlenecks.detection: Break down gateway latency by middleware stage; alert when auth_stage_p99 > 5ms, when auth_cache_hit_ratio < 90%, or when IdP call rate per replica > 500 RPS (indicates cache miss storm).

bottlenecks.title: Deploy-time cold-start and JIT warmup cause rolling error spikes
bottlenecks.trigger: 100 stateless gateway replicas are rolled during each deploy. A newly-started replica needs to (a) fetch the ~5MB rules cache from the config service, (b) establish Redis cluster connections to all 10 shards, and (c) warm JIT/TLS session caches. During the first ~30s it can't serve its share of 10K RPS, but LB's least-connections routing (per the LB component) sends a thundering herd to the zero-connection replica.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sawtooth 5xx/timeout spikes visible at each rolling-restart window; synthetic probes to just-started replicas see 1–3s latency; rules-worker on new replica briefly returns empty rule set causing either fail-open allows or incorrect 429s until first successful poll.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Block readiness probe until (1) rules cache fully populated from config service, (2) Redis cluster slot map loaded, (3) a synthetic warmup of ~1000 requests completes. Combine with LB slow-start (Envoy slow_start_window=60s) so new replicas ramp linearly. Preload Lua scripts via SCRIPT LOAD on Redis connection init to avoid first-request NOSCRIPT round-trip.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when any replica's first-60s error rate > 3× fleet baseline, when rules_cache_loaded=false lasts >10s after process start, or when Redis NOSCRIPT error count > 0 during deploy windows.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the gateway sits here For a rate limiter protecting **1M+ RPS**, the question isn't *whether* to check quotas — it's *where*. You could put the check inside every backend service, but then every team re-implements the same logic, and a buggy service forgets to check at all. The API gateway is the one box every request already passes through for TLS termination and auth, so bolting the rate-limit check on here means **one implementation, one place to upgrade, zero application code changes**. The book's pipeline `auth → rate-limiter → upstream` only works if there's a shared middleware layer — that layer is the gateway. ## What happens without it If rate limiting lived inside each backend, a misbehaving client hammering `/checkout` at 100K RPS would reach the checkout service before being rejected. The user sees slow responses, then errors. The operator sees checkout-service CPU pegged, its DB connection pool exhausted, and *unrelated* endpoints on that service degrading because one noisy neighbor ate all the threads. The whole point of the limiter — **protecting upstream** — is defeated because the damage happened before the check. ## The arithmetic 1M RPS ÷ 100 gateway replicas = **10K RPS per replica**. At 5ms per request, that's 10,000 × 0.005 = **50 concurrent in-flight requests** per replica — trivially under the 3000 concurrency budget. Because the gateway is stateless (all bucket state lives in Redis), you scale by just adding replicas behind the LB. ## Trade-off You've added one network hop (3–10ms) to every request in exchange for uniform enforcement and keeping application services free of cross-cutting boilerplate.

rl.name: Rate Limiter Middleware
rl.summary: Token bucket check implemented via a single Redis Lua script per request — the chapter's preferred algorithm (used by Amazon and Stripe) for its burst tolerance and O(1) memory.

sections.heading: Algorithm (token bucket)
sections.body: Parameters the book names explicitly: **bucket size** (max tokens allowed) and **refill rate** (tokens added per second). Each key `rl:{identity}:{route}` holds `{tokens, last_refill_ts}`. On each request: refill tokens by `elapsed * refill_rate` (clamped to capacity), decrement by 1, deny if <0. How many buckets? The chapter gives three patterns: one bucket per (user, endpoint); one bucket per IP; or a single global bucket for all traffic.

sections.heading: Lua script (atomic)
sections.body:
The chapter names Lua scripts and Redis sorted sets as the two standard fixes for the read-modify-write race between gateway replicas. Sorted sets are the go-to for sliding-window log; Lua is natural for token bucket:
```lua
-- KEYS[1]=bucket ARGV[1]=capacity ARGV[2]=rate ARGV[3]=now
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 't','ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local last = tonumber(b[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[1]), tokens + (tonumber(ARGV[3])-last) * tonumber(ARGV[2]))
if tokens < 1 then redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 't', tokens, 'ts', ARGV[3]) return 0
end
redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 't', tokens-1, 'ts', ARGV[3])
return 1
```

sections.heading: Algorithms compared (per book)
sections.body:
The chapter surveys five algorithms. This middleware runs token bucket; see `alternatives` for the rest.
- **Token bucket**: bursty-friendly, O(1), Amazon/Stripe. Our choice.
- **Leaking bucket**: FIFO queue at fixed rate — smooth output, no burst allowance. Shopify uses this.
- **Fixed window counter**: just INCR+EXPIRE; fails at window boundaries (2x burst).
- **Sliding window log**: Redis sorted set of timestamps; exact but O(N) memory per identity.
- **Sliding window counter**: hybrid — weighted blend of prior + current window. Cloudflare reports only 0.003% misclassification on 400M requests.

sections.heading: Hard vs soft limits
sections.body: The chapter's wrap-up distinguishes hard (must never exceed) from soft (may exceed briefly) rate limits. Soft limits pair well with the throttled queue — a bursty spike is queued rather than 429'd, then drained by upstream as capacity frees.

sections.heading: Fail-open vs fail-closed
sections.body: Requirement #6 in the chapter is high fault tolerance: if Redis is down, the limiter must not take the whole site down. On Redis unavailability: choose fail-open (accept requests) for user-facing APIs to avoid outages, fail-closed for billing/expensive ops. Configurable per rule.

sections.heading: Why token bucket
sections.body: Naturally allows short bursts (up to capacity) while enforcing sustained rate. Sliding-window counter is a cheaper approximation; fixed window permits 2x bursts at boundaries. Leaking bucket sacrifices burst allowance for smooth output.

gained: Exact rate — no burst approximation error
lost: O(N) memory per identity (timestamps of every request)

gained: Cheaper than log; better than fixed window at boundaries
lost: Approximate — assumes uniform distribution within the prior window

gained: Smooth output rate — good for downstream fairness

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key contention on a single Redis slot for abusive identity
bottlenecks.trigger: One api_key or IP sends disproportionate traffic — e.g., 100K+ RPS from a single abusive caller (10% of the 1M RPS fleet). All 100 gateway replicas hash `rl:{identity}:{route}` to the same Redis slot on one of the 10 shards, serializing the Lua EVALSHA through that shard's single-threaded event loop.
bottlenecks.symptom: One Redis shard CPU pegs at 100% while the other 9 idle at ~10%; Lua script p99 climbs from ~2ms to 10–30ms; gateway middleware queue grows and eventually 5xx's on timeout; 429s for the abusive key are delivered slowly, which paradoxically makes things worse because the Retry-After advice is stale by the time it arrives.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a per-gateway-replica local pre-check (in-memory token bucket sized to `limit / N_replicas + slack`) that short-circuits obvious denies before the Redis call — turns hot-key deny traffic into a sub-ms local reject. For extreme abusers, promote to an LB-level deny-list so Redis never sees them. Keep the central Lua check as the source of truth for borderline cases.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on any single Redis slot >70% CPU while cluster average <30%, or on per-identity EVALSHA rate > 10K RPS, or on Lua-script p99 > 5ms (2x the 1–3ms baseline).

bottlenecks.title: Fail-open storm when Redis shard becomes unavailable
bottlenecks.trigger: One of 10 Redis shards goes down (node crash, AZ partition, failover to replica taking 10–30s). Design requirement #6 specifies fail-open for user-facing APIs, so ~10% of identities (those hashed to the failed shard) are suddenly unlimited. If any of those identities was being throttled at high rate, upstream now takes the full unthrottled load.
bottlenecks.symptom: Gateway error logs show Redis connection refused / MOVED errors; limiter metrics show a sudden drop in 429 rate for ~10% of keys; upstream service CPU / DB connection pool spikes on endpoints that were previously rate-limited; during Redis failover the gateway may also briefly fail-closed if configured that way, producing 503 bursts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Configure per-rule fail-mode (fail-closed for billing/expensive ops, fail-open for reads). During fail-open, engage the per-replica local bucket as a degraded-mode fallback so limits are approximately enforced at `limit / 100 replicas`. Use Redis Cluster with 3 replicas per shard and `cluster-require-full-coverage no` so surviving shards keep serving while the failed one fails over (typically <10s with Sentinel/Cluster).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Redis cluster `cluster_state!= ok`, any shard with 0 reachable masters >5s, or sudden drop in `ratelimit_denied_total` rate > 50% vs 5-min baseline (indicates fail-open has kicked in).

bottlenecks.title: Lua script NOSCRIPT + connection-pool exhaustion per gateway replica
bottlenecks.trigger: Each gateway replica drives ~10K RPS, all flowing through the limiter → Redis. If connections to Redis are not pooled (or pool sized < in-flight), every request opens a new TCP+AUTH round-trip adding 1–2ms. Additionally, after a Redis failover or SCRIPT FLUSH the cached script SHA is lost; the first EVALSHA on each connection returns NOSCRIPT and requires a reload, which under load produces a thundering herd of SCRIPT LOAD calls.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis RTT component of limiter latency jumps from 1–3ms to 5–10ms immediately after any Redis maintenance; ephemeral-port exhaustion on gateway hosts (`TIME_WAIT` piles up); bursts of NOSCRIPT errors in limiter logs post-failover with a brief 429/5xx spike; per-replica throughput drops below 10K RPS target.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a fixed-size connection pool per gateway (e.g., 50 connections per replica × 100 replicas = 5K total, well within Redis's 10K concurrency budget) with keep-alive. Preload scripts via `SCRIPT LOAD` on every new connection and on Redis reconnection callback; fall back from EVALSHA to EVAL on NOSCRIPT transparently. Use pipelining where the middleware checks multiple buckets (e.g., per-user AND per-endpoint) in one round-trip.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Redis `connected_clients` > 8K (80% of 10K budget), NOSCRIPT error count > 0 outside deploy windows, or per-replica Redis RTT p99 > 5ms sustained for 1 min.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the rate limiter middleware is here This *is* the thing you're building. Everything else on the diagram — the load balancer, the gateway, Redis, the rules cache — exists to make this one check fast and correct. The problem says "protect APIs at 1M+ RPS with per-user / per-IP / per-API quotas," and that sentence translates directly into: on every single request, decide in a few milliseconds whether this caller has budget left. The middleware is where that decision lives. It's drawn as its own box (rather than folded into the gateway) because the algorithm choice, the Redis Lua script, and the fail-open/fail-closed policy are all distinct design decisions worth reasoning about separately. ## What happens without it Without this check, a single buggy client or abusive scraper can send 100K RPS straight through to your checkout service. The user of that service sees slow pages, then 5xx errors. The operator sees upstream CPU pegged, the DB connection pool exhausted, and — worst of all — *unrelated* endpoints on the same backend degrading because one noisy neighbor ate all the threads. The gateway and Redis look perfectly healthy while the application tier melts. The whole point of the system is to prevent exactly this. ## The arithmetic At **1M RPS fleet-wide**, the middleware runs 1M Lua scripts per second against Redis. With 10 Redis shards, that's 100K ops/sec per shard — well within a single Redis node's ~200K ops/sec ceiling. The token-bucket algorithm is O(1) per check, so 1M RPS costs the same as 1K RPS per identity; only total throughput matters, and sharding handles it linearly. ## Trade-off You've accepted a 1–4ms per-request Redis round-trip on the hot path in exchange for globally-consistent quota enforcement across all 100 gateway replicas.

redis.name: Redis (Token Bucket Store)
redis.summary: Sharded Redis cluster holding per-identity bucket state.

sections.heading: Deployment
sections.body: Redis Cluster with 10 shards, 3 replicas each. Keys hash-slotted by identity so scripts are always single-slot.

sections.heading: Durability
sections.body: AOF `everysec` is enough — a few seconds of lost limiter state post-crash is acceptable; worst case briefly over-admits.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Shard unavailable → middleware fails open (configurable).
- Hot identity (one abusive caller) → single slot hotspot; mitigated by per-instance local pre-check (see alternative).

lost: Limits are per-replica not global → actual allowance = limit * N_replicas
Only viable for soft limits or internal fleets

bottlenecks.title: Single-slot hot key saturates one shard at 100% CPU
bottlenecks.trigger: One abusive identity (api_key or IP) sends 100K+ RPS — 10% of the 1M RPS fleet. All 100 gateway replicas hash `rl:{identity}:{route}` to the same slot on one of the 10 Redis shards, serializing every EVALSHA through that shard's single-threaded event loop. Redis tops out around 200K ops/sec per core, so a single hot identity above ~150K RPS tips the shard.
bottlenecks.symptom: One shard CPU pegs at 100% while the other 9 idle at ~10%; EVALSHA p99 climbs from ~2ms to 10–30ms; gateway middleware backs up and starts 5xx'ing on its own timeout; the very 429s that should throttle the abuser are delivered slowly, making backoff advice stale.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a per-gateway in-memory pre-check token bucket sized to `limit / 100 replicas + slack` to short-circuit obvious denies before Redis is touched; promote repeat abusers to an LB-level deny-list so Redis never sees them; for legitimate hot keys, shard the bucket with a random suffix (e.g., `rl:{id}:{route}:{0..15}`) and sum across sub-buckets in the Lua script.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on any single Redis slot CPU >70% while cluster average <30%, per-key EVALSHA rate >10K RPS (via MONITOR sampling or `redis-cli --hotkeys`), or Lua-script p99 >5ms (2x the 1–3ms baseline).

bottlenecks.title: Shard failover creates 10–30s window of fail-open over-admission
bottlenecks.trigger: One of 10 shards loses its master (node crash, AZ partition, OOM from AOF rewrite). Redis Cluster promotion via Sentinel/cluster-bus typically takes 10–30s. During that window, all gateway replicas serving the ~100K RPS hashed to that shard get connection errors; per requirement #6 the limiter fails open for user-facing APIs, so 10% of identities are suddenly unlimited.
bottlenecks.symptom: Gateway logs show CLUSTERDOWN / MOVED / connection refused for ~10% of keys; limiter denied_total drops ~10% instantly; upstream CPU and DB pool spike on endpoints that were previously rate-limited; if any rule is configured fail-closed, a burst of 503s for that 10% of traffic during the same window.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run 3 replicas per shard with `cluster-require-full-coverage no` and `cluster-replica-validity-factor 0` for faster promotion; keep AOF `everysec` (not `always`) to avoid fsync-induced failovers; engage the per-replica local bucket as degraded-mode enforcement during shard unavailability so limits hold approximately at `limit / 100`; configure fail-closed only for billing/expensive ops.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `cluster_state!= ok`, any shard with 0 reachable masters for >5s, or a sudden drop in `ratelimit_denied_total` rate >50% vs 5-min baseline (indicates fail-open has kicked in).

bottlenecks.title: Connection and ephemeral-port exhaustion from 100 gateways × per-request dialing
bottlenecks.trigger: 100 gateway replicas × ~10K RPS each = 1M connections/sec if each request opens a fresh TCP to Redis. Even with pooling, an undersized pool (e.g., 20 conns/replica) combined with 1–3ms RTT forces queueing at `10K RPS × 2ms = 20 concurrent` — right at the pool ceiling. Post-failover, every connection must re-AUTH and re-SCRIPT LOAD, producing a NOSCRIPT thundering herd.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis `connected_clients` climbs toward the 10K concurrency budget; gateway hosts show `TIME_WAIT` piling up and ephemeral-port exhaustion (`cannot assign requested address`); Redis RTT p99 jumps from 1–3ms to 5–10ms immediately after any maintenance; NOSCRIPT errors spike post-failover with a brief 429/5xx burst.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Fixed-size pool of 50 keep-alive connections per gateway replica (50 × 100 = 5K, half the 10K budget); preload the Lua script via `SCRIPT LOAD` on every new/reconnected connection with transparent EVALSHA→EVAL fallback on NOSCRIPT; pipeline multi-bucket checks (per-user + per-endpoint) in one round-trip; raise `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range` and enable `tcp_tw_reuse` on gateway hosts.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Redis `connected_clients` >8K (80% of budget), NOSCRIPT error count >0 outside deploy windows, per-replica Redis RTT p99 >5ms sustained for 1 min, or host-level `netstat` TIME_WAIT count >20K.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Redis is here for this rate limiter The whole point of this system is enforcing quotas **globally** — if your API key has 100 req/min, that limit has to hold whether your requests land on gateway replica #3 or #87. With **100 gateway replicas** all checking quotas independently, you need a shared source of truth that every replica can read and update atomically. Redis gives you exactly that: fast in-memory counters (bucket state is just `{tokens, last_refill_ts}`, ~100 bytes per key) with single-threaded Lua execution that prevents two replicas from both "spending" the last token at the same time. ## What happens without it If each gateway kept bucket state locally in memory, a client's effective quota would silently become `limit × 100 replicas`. A "100 req/min" key could actually send 10,000 req/min by spraying across replicas. The user wouldn't notice — their app just works *too well*. The operator would see upstream services getting hammered at rates that shouldn't be possible given the configured limits, dashboards showing 429s nearly never fire, and the downstream DB pool exhausting during a scraper attack that the limiter was supposed to stop. ## The arithmetic At **1M RPS fleet-wide**, every request does one Lua script call against Redis. Spread across **10 shards**, that's 100K ops/sec per shard — comfortably under Redis's ~200K ops/sec per-core ceiling. Memory is a non-issue: 50K active buckets × 100B ≈ **5 MB total**, which fits in L3 cache on a single node. ## Trade-off You've added a 1–3ms network round-trip to every API call and a new piece of stateful infrastructure to operate — in exchange for quota enforcement that's actually correct across the fleet.

cfg.name: Config Service (Rules on Disk)
cfg.summary: Authoritative store of rate-limit rules — per the book, rules are written in config files and persisted on disk, then pulled by background workers into an in-memory cache on each limiter replica.

sections.heading: Rule format (Lyft-style YAML, per book)
sections.body:
The chapter reproduces two Lyft ratelimit examples verbatim:
```yaml
domain: messaging
descriptors: - key: message_type value: marketing rate_limit: unit: day requests_per_unit: 5
```
```yaml
domain: auth
descriptors: - key: auth_type value: login rate_limit: unit: minute requests_per_unit: 5
```
Rules are stored on disk (YAML files in git/object storage) and reloaded by a background worker.

sections.heading: API
sections.body: `GET /rules?version=...` returns rule deltas. Rules: `{domain, descriptors, unit, requests_per_unit, action}`.

sections.heading: Propagation
sections.body: Background rules-worker polls every 5s and writes into the local rules cache; global update within 5–10s. For faster push, use a pub/sub channel on Redis or etcd watch.

sections.heading: Storage
sections.body: Postgres or git-backed YAML for the authoritative rule set; file-system or in-memory cache on limiter replicas.

bottlenecks.title: Polling thundering herd on rule publish
bottlenecks.trigger: All 100 gateway rules-workers poll every 5s on loosely-aligned clocks. When an operator publishes a rule change, cache-busting (ETag mismatch) causes most/all 100 workers to request the full ~5MB rule set within a narrow window — transient spike from the steady-state 20 RPS baseline to 100 concurrent full-payload fetches (~500MB egress in seconds).
bottlenecks.symptom: Config service CPU/bandwidth spike immediately after any rule publish; p99 fetch latency jumps from 3–10ms to hundreds of ms or timeouts; some gateway workers fail their poll and serve stale rules for an extra 5–10s; on-call sees correlated dashboards between 'rule edit' events and config-service saturation.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Serve rule deltas keyed by version (`GET /rules?since=<v>`) instead of full snapshots; add jitter to the 5s poll interval (e.g., 5s ± 1s uniform) so workers desynchronize; put a CDN or in-cluster HTTP cache (Varnish/nginx with 1s TTL on the version endpoint) in front of the config service; for faster and cheaper propagation, migrate to etcd watch or Redis pub/sub as the alternative notes.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on config-service RPS > 5× baseline (>100 RPS) for >10s, egress bandwidth spike >100MB/s, or p99 `GET /rules` latency >50ms; track the ratio of full-snapshot to delta responses and alert if full-snapshot rate >10/min outside of deploy windows.

bottlenecks.title: Stale rules window after publish due to 5s poll interval
bottlenecks.trigger: Design states 'global update within 5–10s' because rules-workers poll every 5s. An urgent rule change — e.g., emergency tightening of a limit to stop an active abuse incident, or widening a limit during a legitimate traffic surge — cannot propagate faster than the poll cycle. Across 100 replicas with unsynchronized poll offsets, the last replica to see the change may lag up to 10s.
bottlenecks.symptom: Ops publishes a new quota at T=0 but abusive traffic continues to be allowed (or legit traffic 429'd) for up to 10s; different gateway replicas disagree on the effective limit during the propagation window, producing seemingly random 429/200 flapping for the same client; incident MTTR is bounded below by rule-propagation latency.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Expose a push/watch channel (etcd watch or Redis pub/sub on a `rules-updated` topic) so workers invalidate and refetch within <1s of publish; keep the 5s poll as a safety net for missed events; add a manual `/rules/reload` admin endpoint broadcast via the same channel for emergency changes; version-stamp rules and surface `rules_version` as a gateway metric so drift across replicas is observable.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit `rules_version_age_seconds` per replica; alert if any replica's version lags the config-service current version by >15s, or if the spread of `rules_version` across the 100 replicas is non-zero for >10s after a known publish event.

bottlenecks.title: Config service unavailability causes degraded rule freshness and blocks deploys
bottlenecks.trigger: Config service is a single logical dependency for rule distribution. If it goes down (Postgres outage, git backend unreachable, deploy gone wrong — failureRate 0.0005 at ~20 RPS baseline = background errors, but a full outage is the risk), the 100 rules-workers can't refresh. Worse, per the gateway component's cold-start bottleneck, new gateway replicas block readiness on populating the rules cache from this service — so a config-service outage during a gateway deploy halts the deploy.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rules-worker logs fill with fetch errors; `rules_version_age_seconds` climbs unbounded across all 100 replicas; rule changes made during the outage don't take effect anywhere; any gateway rolling restart stalls because new replicas never become ready; operators lose the ability to respond to abuse via rule changes precisely when they may need it most.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run config service as HA (≥3 replicas behind a LB, stateless read path backed by replicated Postgres or git mirror); have rules-workers persist the last-known-good rule set to local disk and load from disk on startup so gateway cold-start doesn't hard-depend on config service reachability; fall back to 'serve last known rules indefinitely' (already designed) and surface staleness as a metric rather than failing; for DR, mirror rule YAML to S3/object storage as a secondary source.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on config-service availability <99.9% over 5min, any rules-worker with >60s since last successful fetch, gateway readiness probe failures attributed to 'rules cache not populated', and absence of successful `GET /rules` from >10% of gateway replicas in any 30s window.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the config service is here For a rate limiter protecting **1M+ RPS across ~50K distinct quotas**, somebody has to answer the question: *what is the limit for this (api_key, endpoint) pair?* That answer has to be authored by humans (product/ops decide "marketing messages capped at 5/day, login attempts at 5/min"), version-controlled so changes are auditable, and distributed to all 100 gateway replicas so they enforce identically. The config service is the authoritative home for those rules — the Lyft-style YAML files sitting on disk or in git. Without a dedicated home for rules, you'd be hardcoding limits into gateway code and redeploying every time marketing wants a new quota. ## What happens without it If rules lived only in each gateway's config file, changing a limit means a rolling deploy of 100 replicas — 10+ minutes during which different replicas enforce different limits. Worse, during an active abuse incident when you need to *tighten* a quota right now, the user whose account is being scraped keeps getting hammered while you wait for CI. The operator sees inconsistent 429 rates across replicas; the abuser sees a slow-moving target that's easy to outpace. ## The arithmetic The design notes **<100 rule updates/minute globally** and **rules-workers polling every 5s**, so config-service load is `100 replicas / 5s = 20 RPS`. That's negligible — one small Postgres instance handles it — which is exactly why it's safe to centralize: the hot path (1M RPS) never touches it, only the cold rules-refresh loop does. ## Trade-off You've accepted 5–10s propagation delay for rule changes in exchange for a single source of truth that's cheap to operate and git-auditable.

rulescache.name: Rules Cache (in-memory)
rulescache.summary: Per-limiter in-memory copy of the authoritative rule set so hot-path lookups avoid the config service.

sections.heading: Why this is a distinct component (per book)
sections.body: Chapter 4's detailed-design section explicitly shows 'Rules → Workers → Cache → Rate limiter' as two hops: rules live on disk, workers pull them, the limiter reads from the cache on every request. Skipping the cache would add a network hop per API call, which violates the chapter's low-latency requirement.

sections.heading: Lookup cost
sections.body: Hash map keyed by `(domain, descriptor)` → rule struct. O(1), memory-local, sub-microsecond.

sections.heading: Eviction
sections.body: Rule set is small (~50K rules → ~5 MB) — keep the whole set resident; no eviction needed. Version counter lets readers see a consistent snapshot.

bottlenecks.title: Read-during-swap tearing when worker replaces the rule set
bottlenecks.trigger: Rules worker refreshes every 5s while the hot path reads the cache at 10K RPS per replica (1M RPS / 100 replicas). If the worker mutates the hashmap in place (e.g., clear + repopulate ~50K entries), concurrent readers observe a partially-populated map during the ~1–10ms rewrite window, yielding spurious cache misses on ~50–100 requests per refresh per replica.
bottlenecks.symptom: Transient spikes of 'rule not found' every 5s synchronized with the poll cycle; limiter falls back to default limits or fails open for a burst of requests; in race-y languages a map-concurrent-access panic crashes the gateway replica outright.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use an atomic pointer swap (Go `atomic.Value`, Java `AtomicReference`, Rust `ArcSwap`) — worker builds a fresh immutable hashmap off-path, then CAS-swaps the pointer in one instruction. Readers dereference the pointer once per request and hold a stable snapshot. Never mutate the live map.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `rules_cache_miss_total` rate >0 when `rules_version` is stable, correlate miss spikes against `rules_worker_refresh_timestamp`, and panic-log any concurrent-map-access stack trace.

bottlenecks.title: Version skew across replicas produces inconsistent 429 decisions
bottlenecks.trigger: Each of the 100 replicas runs an independent 5s poll with unsynchronized offsets, so at any instant the 100 caches may hold up to two different rule versions for up to 5–10s after a publish. A client's request routed via LB least-connections can hit a replica with the old limit and get allowed, then the next request hits an updated replica and gets 429.
bottlenecks.symptom: Client sees flapping 200/429 responses for the same endpoint at the same offered rate immediately after a rule change; support reports 'my new limit didn't take effect' for some users but not others; `X-Ratelimit-Limit` header value differs across responses within the same second.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Stamp each cache entry with a `rules_version` and expose it as a gateway response header and Prometheus gauge; on rule publish, trigger an out-of-band pub/sub invalidation (Redis PUBLISH on `rules-updated`) so all 100 caches refresh within <1s instead of waiting for the 5s poll; keep the periodic poll as a safety net.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit `rules_cache_version` per replica; alert when the max−min spread across replicas is non-zero for >10s, or when >5% of replicas lag the config-service current version by more than one generation.

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded growth if rule set scales beyond the 5 MB assumption
bottlenecks.trigger: Design assumes ~50K rules × ~100B ≈ 5 MB resident, 'no eviction needed.' If product expands to per-user-per-endpoint rules (e.g., 10M users × 10 endpoints = 100M entries), the cache balloons to ~10 GB per replica — 2000× the budget — exceeding gateway heap and stalling GC.
bottlenecks.symptom: Gateway replica RSS climbs over days/weeks; JVM/Go GC pause p99 rises from sub-ms into tens of ms, dragging the limiter's 1–4ms budget; eventually OOMKill and replica flap; rules-worker refresh latency grows from 10–50ms to seconds as it deserializes the full set.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce a hard cap (e.g., 200K entries, 50 MB) in the rules worker with a loud alert if exceeded; for high-cardinality rules, switch to a two-tier design — coarse rules in-memory, fine-grained rules resolved on-demand from Redis with a short TTL LRU; reject config service responses that exceed the cap rather than loading them.
bottlenecks.detection: Gauge `rules_cache_entry_count` and `rules_cache_bytes`; alert at 50% (25K entries / 2.5 MB) as an early warning and at 80% as page; track gateway heap RSS trend and GC pause p99 against a 5ms SLO.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the rules cache is here For a rate limiter at **1M+ RPS**, every single request has to answer one question before anything else: *what is the limit for this (api_key, endpoint)?* The authoritative answer lives in the config service — YAML files on disk, maybe behind Postgres or git. But calling that service on every request would add a network hop (3–10ms) to a hot path that's budgeted at 1–4ms. The rules cache exists so the limiter can answer that question in **under a microsecond** with an in-memory hashmap lookup, letting the real work (the Redis token-bucket call) happen inside the latency budget. ## What happens without it Without the cache, every one of the 1M requests per second hits the config service directly. The user sees request latency climb from a few ms to tens of ms, and p99 gets ugly during any config-service hiccup. The operator sees the config service's modest Postgres or git backend pegged at CPU ceiling — it was sized for ~20 RPS of rule refreshes, not 1M RPS of quota lookups. Worst: if the config service briefly slows or fails, the limiter itself stalls, and the gateway starts timing out requests that should have been allowed. ## The arithmetic The rule set is ~50K rules × ~100B = **~5 MB** per replica. That fits entirely in L3 cache on a modern CPU, so a lookup is effectively free (sub-microsecond). Meanwhile the config service sees `100 replicas / 5s poll = 20 RPS` instead of 1,000,000 RPS — a 50,000× load reduction. ## Trade-off You accept 5–10s of rule-change propagation delay so the hot path never touches the network for rule lookups.

rulesworker.name: Rules Worker
rulesworker.summary: Background goroutine/process that periodically pulls rules from the config service / disk and refreshes the in-memory rules cache.

sections.heading: Role (per book)
sections.body: Chapter 4 Figure 4-13: 'Workers frequently pull rules from the disk and store them in the cache.' This keeps the hot request path free of any off-box lookup.

sections.heading: Poll interval
sections.body: 5 seconds is a reasonable default — trades freshness vs. config-service load. On a watch-capable store (etcd/Consul) switch to push for sub-second propagation.

sections.heading: Failure mode
sections.body: If the worker can't reach the config service it keeps serving the last-known rule set — rules freshness degrades gracefully, limiter does not fail.

bottlenecks.title: Synchronized poll storm hammers config service on rule publish
bottlenecks.trigger: All 100 rules-workers poll every 5s; if process start times cluster (e.g., after a fleet-wide rolling deploy or a simultaneous rule publish that invalidates cached ETags), up to 100 workers fetch the full ~5MB rule set within a narrow window — bursting from the steady 20 RPS baseline to 100 concurrent fetches and ~500MB egress in seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Config service CPU and egress bandwidth spike every 5s or immediately after rule publishes; some workers time out their 10–50ms fetch and serve stale rules for an extra 5–10s; gateway replicas briefly disagree on effective limits producing 200/429 flapping.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add ±20% jitter to the 5s poll interval (uniform 4–6s) so the 100 workers desynchronize; request deltas via `GET /rules?since=<version>` instead of full snapshots; cache responses at an in-cluster HTTP layer (Varnish/nginx, 1s TTL) in front of the config service; switch to etcd watch or Redis pub/sub for push-based propagation as the component's alternative notes.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when config-service RPS > 5× baseline (>100 RPS) for >10s, when full-snapshot fetches exceed 10/min outside deploy windows, or when the standard deviation of worker poll timestamps across the fleet collapses below 500ms (indicates synchronization).

bottlenecks.title: Silent staleness when config service is unreachable
bottlenecks.trigger: Worker's documented failure mode is 'keep serving last-known rules' — failureRate 0.001 at ~0.2 polls/sec per replica means background errors are expected, but a sustained config-service outage (Postgres down, git backend unreachable) means no replica refreshes for the duration. Combined with new gateway cold-starts blocking readiness on rule fetches, deploys during the outage stall entirely.
bottlenecks.symptom: `rules_version_age_seconds` climbs unbounded across all 100 replicas with no alert firing because the limiter itself keeps serving; urgent rule changes (e.g., tightening a quota to stop active abuse) don't take effect anywhere; gateway rolling restarts stall because new replicas never reach ready state; operators lose incident-response tooling precisely when they need it.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Persist last-known-good rules to local disk after every successful poll so cold-start doesn't hard-depend on config-service reachability; mirror rule YAML to S3/object storage as a secondary fetch source with automatic failover; emit `rules_stale_seconds` metric and page when >60s; implement exponential backoff (1s → 30s cap) on fetch errors to avoid amplifying the outage.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on any worker with >60s since last successful fetch, config-service availability <99.9% over 5min, >10% of workers failing consecutive polls within any 30s window, or gateway readiness-probe failures tagged 'rules cache not populated'.

bottlenecks.title: Cache-swap pause blocks or tears hot-path reads during refresh
bottlenecks.trigger: Worker refreshes ~50K rules (~5MB) every 5s while the hot path reads the cache at 10K RPS per replica. If the refresh uses a naive lock or mutates the hashmap in place, the 10–50ms worker service-time window overlaps with ~100–500 in-flight lookups that either block or observe a partially-populated map.
bottlenecks.symptom: Every 5s, a burst of 'rule not found' cache misses causes the limiter to fall back to defaults or fail open; gateway p99 shows a 5s-periodic sawtooth of 10–50ms latency spikes; in race-prone runtimes a concurrent-map-access panic crashes the replica outright.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Build the new rule set in an off-path immutable structure, then atomically swap the pointer (Go `atomic.Value`, Java `AtomicReference`, Rust `ArcSwap`) in a single CAS instruction — readers dereference once per request and hold a stable snapshot; never mutate the live map; verify new rule set size/version before swap to reject corrupt responses.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `rules_cache_miss_total` rate >0 when `rules_version` is stable, correlate miss/latency spikes against `rules_worker_refresh_timestamp` (should be uncorrelated), and fail-fast log any concurrent-map-access stack trace.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the rules worker is here For a rate limiter at **1M+ RPS**, every request needs to look up "what's the limit for this api_key on this endpoint?" That answer lives authoritatively in the config service (YAML on disk, backed by Postgres or git). But you absolutely cannot call the config service on the hot path — that would add a 3–10ms network hop to every one of the 1M requests/second, and it would crush the config service's modest backend. The rules worker is the background process that bridges those two worlds: it fetches from the config service on a slow cadence and writes into the in-memory rules cache that the hot path actually reads from. ## What happens without it Without a worker, you've got two bad options. Either the limiter calls the config service per request (latency explodes, config DB melts under 1M RPS it was never sized for), or rules are loaded once at startup and never refreshed (operators publish a new quota to stop an active abuser and… nothing happens until the next deploy). The user sees either slow requests or an abuse incident that drags on; the operator sees a config service pegged at CPU limit or rule changes that mysteriously don't take effect. ## The arithmetic With **100 gateway replicas polling every 5 seconds**, the config service sees `100 / 5 = 20 RPS` — negligible, one small Postgres handles it easily. Compare that to the 1,000,000 RPS the hot path handles: the worker achieves a **50,000× load reduction** on the config service. ## Trade-off You accept up to 5–10 seconds of rule-change propagation delay in exchange for keeping the hot path purely local.

throttledq.name: Throttled Request Queue
throttledq.summary: Optional queue for rate-limited requests the chapter mentions — instead of dropping, enqueue for later processing (e.g., order submission under load).

sections.heading: Why this exists (per book)
sections.body: Chapter 4's 'Exceeding the rate limit' section: 'Depending on the use cases, we may enqueue the rate-limited requests to be processed later. For example, if some orders are rate limited due to system overload, we may keep those orders to be processed later.' This is the soft-limit behaviour distinguished from the hard-limit drop.

sections.heading: When to enable
sections.body:
- Critical business flows where dropping is worse than delay (checkout, payment retries, webhook deliveries)
- Do NOT use for idempotent GETs — clients should just retry.
- Pair with a deadline header so stale items are dropped at dequeue time.

sections.heading: Operational risk
sections.body: A queue in front of a rate limiter is effectively a leaking bucket. It protects upstream but delays the user. Monitor queue depth — a chronically full queue means the limits are set wrong.

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded queue growth when upstream drain rate stays below enqueue rate
bottlenecks.trigger: Soft-limit enqueue path parks requests whose arrival rate exceeds per-identity token-bucket refill. If 1% of the 1M RPS fleet (10K RPS) is soft-limited and upstream can only drain the excess at ~1K RPS (it's already near its 2000-concurrency ceiling at 10–50ms service time), queue depth grows at 9K items/sec — 540K items/min — blowing past the 50K concurrency budget in under 6 seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Queue depth graph climbs monotonically; dequeued items are already past their deadline and dropped wastefully; clients that got 202 Accepted never see their work completed; memory/disk on the queue broker (Kafka/SQS/Redis Streams) fills up; on-call sees 'queue full' or broker OOM alerts while gateway and Redis look healthy.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Hard cap queue depth per (domain, descriptor) at e.g. 10× steady-state drain rate (so ~10s of buffering), and return 429 (not 202) when the cap is hit — degrade soft-limit to hard-limit under sustained overload. Enforce a per-item deadline header (e.g., 30s) and drop-on-dequeue if expired. Autoscale upstream off queue depth, not CPU, so drain rate tracks offered load.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when queue_depth > 5000 sustained 30s, when enqueue_rate / dequeue_rate > 1.2 for 1min, or when deadline_expired_drops_total > 100/min (indicates items rotting in queue).

bottlenecks.title: Misuse on idempotent GETs inflates queue and defeats its purpose
bottlenecks.trigger: Design explicitly says 'Do NOT use for idempotent GETs — clients should just retry,' but without enforcement any rule author can flip a read endpoint to soft-limit mode. At 1M RPS fleet-wide with ~50K rules, a single misconfigured high-traffic GET rule (say 50K RPS of that identity) enqueuing on denial floods the queue with work that the client is already retrying independently — 2× amplification.
bottlenecks.symptom: Queue depth grows during traffic surges on read-heavy endpoints; upstream sees duplicate requests (one from client retry via Retry-After, one from queue drain); business metrics show double-counted reads; clients occasionally get stale data from queue-drained GETs that raced their own retry.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce at rule-validation time in the config service: reject rules with `action: enqueue` whose descriptor matches idempotent method patterns (GET/HEAD) unless an explicit `override: true` flag is set. Require an idempotency key on every enqueued request so dequeue-time dedup drops duplicates against a short-TTL Redis set.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit queue_enqueue_total labelled by http_method; alert if enqueue rate for GET/HEAD > 0 in production, or if idempotency_key_collision_rate > 1% at dequeue time (indicates client + queue both processing same request).

bottlenecks.title: Dequeue worker stampede re-exhausts the token bucket, causing drain stalls
bottlenecks.trigger: Dequeue workers drain the queue toward upstream, but each dequeued request must still pass the token-bucket check (the original quota hasn't gone away). If workers pull eagerly after a burst subsides, they hit the same Redis Lua script for the same identity at high concurrency, re-denying most items and either re-queueing (infinite loop) or dropping them. At 50K queue concurrency × single hot identity, this pins one Redis shard at 100% CPU just on dequeue retries.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis shard CPU spikes correlate with queue-drain start rather than client arrivals; dequeue_retry_count per item climbs into the tens; queue depth oscillates instead of monotonically decreasing; limiter p99 degrades for unrelated identities sharing the same shard.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Dequeue workers should pace themselves to the bucket refill rate: use the token-bucket's `requests_per_unit` from the rules cache to set a per-identity drain throttle (e.g., token semaphore). On Redis-level deny at dequeue, re-queue with a delay equal to `X-Ratelimit-Retry-After` rather than immediately. Cap per-identity in-flight dequeues at `requests_per_unit × 1s` so workers never outrun the refill.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on dequeue_retry_count_p99 > 3, on per-identity dequeue_deny_ratio > 50% (workers pulling faster than bucket refills), or on Redis shard CPU correlating with queue-drain events rather than client-arrival events.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the throttled queue is here For a rate limiter at **1M+ RPS**, the default answer when a bucket is empty is simple: return 429 and let the client retry. But some requests are too important to drop. If a user clicks "Place Order" during a Black Friday surge and their api_key is momentarily over quota, telling them "try again in 30 seconds" is worse than just *holding* their request and processing it when capacity frees up. The throttled queue is the optional soft-limit path the book calls out for exactly this case — the gateway returns `202 Accepted`, parks the work, and drains it against upstream as tokens refill. ## What happens without it Without the queue, every bucket-exhausted request becomes a hard 429. The user sees their checkout fail and either gives up or mashes the retry button — which, per the client component's analysis, amplifies load 5–10× on the very endpoint you were trying to protect. The operator sees a spike in abandoned carts correlated with 429s, and upstream still gets hammered by the retry storm anyway. You paid the cost of rejection without getting the benefit of smoothed load. ## The arithmetic Upstream is budgeted at **2000 concurrency at 10–50ms**, giving it roughly `2000 / 0.03s ≈ 66K RPS` sustained drain. If a soft-limited identity briefly arrives at 76K RPS, queuing the 10K/sec excess for ~10 seconds (100K items, well under the queue's 50K concurrency budget if drained promptly) lets upstream catch up without dropping any order. ## Trade-off You've accepted added latency and a new failure mode (queue can grow unbounded) in exchange for not dropping business-critical requests during short bursts.

upstream.name: Upstream Service
upstream.summary: The actual API the gateway protects; only reached if the limiter allows.

sections.heading: Role in this design
sections.body: Models the downstream application. Limiter's whole purpose is to keep this tier healthy.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body: Cost/latency of upstream is exactly what the limiter is protecting — if upstream is 50ms, saving 1% of its load pays for the limiter many times over.

bottlenecks.title: Concurrency ceiling hit when limiter fails open during Redis shard outage
bottlenecks.trigger: Upstream is sized for 2000 concurrency at 10–50ms service time, giving a sustained ceiling of ~66K RPS (well below the 1M RPS fleet arrival rate — the limiter is doing heavy lifting). When one of 10 Redis shards fails and the limiter fails open per requirement #6, ~10% of previously-throttled identities become unlimited; if those identities were being denied at even 50K RPS cumulatively, upstream suddenly absorbs load it was never provisioned for.
bottlenecks.symptom: Upstream in_flight jumps from steady-state ~500–1000 to 2000 within seconds; new requests queue then 5xx with connection-refused or request-timeout; DB connection pool exhausted; p99 latency climbs from 50ms into seconds; gateway starts returning 503s alongside normal 429s, confusing on-call about root cause.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Engage per-replica local-bucket degraded-mode enforcement during Redis shard unavailability (already designed at the limiter) so limits hold approximately at `limit / 100 replicas` instead of going fully unlimited; add an upstream-side adaptive concurrency limiter (Netflix concurrency-limits or Envoy gradient controller) as last-line defense sized to 1800 (90% of 2000); configure fail-closed on endpoints whose upstream cost is high (payments, writes) and fail-open only on cheap reads.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on upstream in_flight > 1600 (80% of 2000 concurrency) for 30s, upstream p99 > 2× baseline (>100ms), or sudden drop in gateway `ratelimit_denied_total` rate >50% (indicates fail-open engaged) correlated with upstream saturation.

bottlenecks.title: Throttled-queue drain overwhelms upstream when drain rate mis-sized
bottlenecks.trigger: Throttled queue (50K concurrency budget) drains into upstream, but upstream only sustains ~66K RPS total (2000 concurrency ÷ 30ms avg). If drain workers pull eagerly after a burst — e.g., 500K queued items from a 10-second surge — and aren't paced to token-bucket refill rates, they can saturate the remaining upstream headroom above organic 1M RPS × allowed fraction, leaving zero capacity for fresh non-throttled requests.
bottlenecks.symptom: Upstream p99 spikes whenever queue depth decreases rapidly; fresh requests from well-behaved clients see latency/5xx spikes that correlate with queue-drain events rather than client arrivals; business metrics show order processing batching in bursts rather than smoothly; queue oscillates as drained items are re-denied and re-queued.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap per-identity dequeue concurrency at `requests_per_unit × 1s` using the rules-cache token-bucket config so drain paces to refill rate; size global drain workers so drain-rate + organic-allowed-rate ≤ 80% of upstream's 66K RPS ceiling (leave 20% headroom); use bounded concurrency limiter on the queue→upstream path independent of the 50K queue concurrency; honor `Retry-After` on Redis deny at dequeue (requeue with delay, don't spin).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when upstream_rps attributable to queue drain > 30% of upstream capacity (>20K RPS from queue drain alone), when upstream p99 correlates with queue_dequeue_rate rather than client_arrival_rate, or when dequeue_retry_count_p99 > 3.

bottlenecks.title: Slow-dependency amplification cascading back through the gateway concurrency budget
bottlenecks.trigger: Upstream's 10–50ms service time assumes healthy dependencies (DB, cache, downstream services). A GC pause, DB lock, or slow dependency pushes p99 from 50ms to 300ms. At the allowed rate (~10K RPS per gateway replica × 100 replicas), upstream in-flight climbs from ~500 to `allowed_rps × 0.3s` — easily blowing past 2000 concurrency. Simultaneously, gateway replicas with concurrency=3000 fill up waiting on upstream (per the gateway's own bottleneck #1), propagating failure upstream-ward.
bottlenecks.symptom: Upstream CPU looks moderate but in_flight saturates; requests queue in TCP accept backlogs; gateway p99 climbs into seconds; LB marks gateway replicas unhealthy and shifts load, cascading saturation; limiter metrics look perfectly normal (allowing expected rates) while the whole stack behind it melts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set explicit per-upstream-instance max_concurrent_requests (e.g., Envoy cluster circuit-breaker at 1800 — 90% of 2000); enable request hedging/deadline propagation from gateway (deadline header) so upstream drops requests already past their client-side timeout; add a fast-acting load shedder on upstream that returns 503+Retry-After when in_flight > 80% ceiling so the limiter/gateway can convert it into client backoff; autoscale upstream off in_flight concurrency, not just CPU.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on upstream in_flight > 1600 sustained 30s, upstream p99 latency > 2× 7-day baseline, dependency RTT p99 > expected (e.g., DB query p99 > 20ms), or when gateway in_flight rises while gateway CPU stays flat (indicates waiting-on-upstream, not gateway-bound work).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the upstream service is on this diagram For a distributed rate limiter protecting **1M+ RPS**, the upstream service is *the thing being protected*. It's drawn explicitly on the diagram because without it there's no reason for the limiter to exist — every other box (load balancer, gateway, Redis, rules cache) is infrastructure whose only job is to keep this tier healthy. The upstream is sized for **2000 concurrent requests at 10–50ms service time**, which is dramatically less than the 1M RPS arriving at the edge. That gap *is* the design problem: the limiter exists to bridge it. ## What happens without the limiter in front If 1M RPS hit upstream directly, you'd see request queues balloon, DB connection pools exhaust, p99 latency climb from 50ms into multi-second territory, and eventually 5xx cascades as the service runs out of threads. The user sees their order fail or the page hang. The operator sees upstream CPU pegged, alerts firing on downstream dependencies (DB, cache), and — frustratingly — *legitimate* traffic failing alongside abusive traffic because nothing has distinguished them. ## The arithmetic Upstream sustains roughly `2000 concurrency ÷ 0.03s avg = ~66K RPS`. Arrival is 1M RPS. The limiter must shed at least `1,000,000 − 66,000 = 934,000 RPS` to keep upstream alive — meaning **~93% of traffic under worst-case abuse must be rejected before ever reaching this box**. That's why a 1–4ms Redis check on the hot path is a bargain. ## Trade-off The designer accepted upstream as a hard capacity ceiling rather than over-provisioning it, because scaling the limiter is cheaper than scaling the application tier.

operations.title: Request allowed (tokens available)
operations.name: Request allowed (tokens available)
operations.description: Normal path: limiter loads the rule from its local rules cache, runs the token-bucket Lua script against Redis, decrements a token, and forwards upstream.

steps.title: Client calls POST /v1/messages with API key
steps.action: 3rd-party integration fires a message-send request. The SDK attaches the caller's API key in the Authorization header so the limiter can attribute the request to the right token bucket.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /v1/messages HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_9f2a7b3c
Content-Type: application/json {"to":"+15551234567","body":"hello"}
steps.note: The caller's identity (api_key) is what the limiter hashes to a bucket — not the IP. IP fallback is only for anonymous endpoints.

steps.title: Load balancer terminates TLS, picks a gateway replica
steps.action: Least-connections across 100 gateway replicas. No stickiness needed because bucket state lives in Redis, so any replica can answer.
steps.codeOrCommand:
upstream = pool.pick(algo="least_conn", healthy_only=True)
# gw-42 has fewest in-flight → forward there
forward(req → gw-42)

steps.title: Gateway runs auth, hands off to rate-limit middleware
steps.action: Pipeline is `auth → rate-limiter → upstream`. Auth resolves the bearer token to api_key=acme_prod via a locally-cached JWKS verify (hit rate >95%) and tags the request context before the limiter runs.

steps.title: Rate-limit middleware resolves the rule for (identity, route)
steps.action: Middleware builds the bucket key and asks the in-memory rules cache which quota applies. No network hop here — this is a sub-microsecond hashmap lookup.

steps.title: Rules cache returns the token-bucket config (O(1))
steps.action: Hashmap lookup against the atomically-swapped immutable rule snapshot loaded by the rules worker. Returns capacity=100, refill=100/60s (100 req/min).
steps.note: Capacity is the burst allowance; refill_rate smooths sustained load. Token bucket (book's chosen algorithm) lets a well-behaved client burst up to 100 and then settle to ~100/min.

steps.title: Lua token-bucket script runs atomically on the owning shard
steps.action: EVALSHA against the preloaded script. Key hash-slots `rl:acme_prod:POST /v1/messages` to shard 3. Redis's single-threaded event loop guarantees the read-modify-write is race-free across all 100 gateway replicas.
steps.codeOrCommand:
-- KEYS[1]=bucket ARGV[1]=capacity ARGV[2]=rate ARGV[3]=now
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 't','ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local last = tonumber(b[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[1]), tokens + (tonumber(ARGV[3])-last) * tonumber(ARGV[2]))
if tokens < 1 then redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 't', tokens, 'ts', ARGV[3]) return 0
end
redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 't', tokens-1, 'ts', ARGV[3])
return 1

rl:acme_prod:POST /v1/messages.note: refilled by 1.667s * 1.6667/s ≈ 2.78, clamped to capacity logic; then -1 for this request

steps.title: Upstream messaging service processes the request
steps.action: With the quota check passed, the gateway proxies to the messaging backend. Typical service time 10–50ms (DB write + downstream SMS vendor call).

steps.title: Gateway attaches rate-limit headers to the response
steps.action: Per book p.64, the gateway annotates every response (allow or deny) with X-Ratelimit-Limit and X-Ratelimit-Remaining so well-behaved SDKs can self-pace.
steps.codeOrCommand:
res.headers['X-Ratelimit-Limit'] = rule.requests_per_unit // 100
res.headers['X-Ratelimit-Remaining'] = Math.floor(tokens_remaining) // 74
return res

steps.title: LB wraps response in TLS and sends to client
steps.action: Return path over the existing connection — no routing decision, no new handshake thanks to HTTP/2 multiplexing.

steps.title: Client receives 200, reads remaining budget
steps.action: SDK records X-Ratelimit-Remaining=74 into its client-side meter so it can self-throttle before hitting 429. End-to-end latency on the happy path is typically 15–60ms (limiter overhead is ~2ms of that).

operations.title: Request rate-limited (429 + headers)
operations.name: Request rate-limited (429 + headers)
operations.description: Bucket empty; gateway returns 429 with X-Ratelimit-Limit / X-Ratelimit-Remaining / X-Ratelimit-Retry-After headers and does NOT touch upstream.

steps.title: Client bursts past quota
steps.action: A poorly-coded integration fires its 101st request this minute against a 100/min quota. Same endpoint, same api_key as the allowed path — only the bucket state has changed.

steps.title: LB forwards to a gateway replica
steps.action: Same routing as the allow path. The LB can't know this request will be denied — that decision lives at the limiter.

steps.title: Gateway auth succeeds, enters limiter middleware
steps.action: Auth is fine — the api_key is valid. Quota is a separate concern that the next middleware enforces.
steps.codeOrCommand:
ctx.principal = auth.verify(req.headers.authorization) // acme_prod
await rateLimiter.check(ctx)

steps.title: Limiter builds bucket key, looks up rule
steps.action: Same local rule resolution as the allow path. This step never reads Redis.
steps.codeOrCommand:
bucket_key = `rl:acme_prod:POST /v1/messages`
rule = rulesCache.lookup("messaging", "api_key:acme_prod")

steps.title: Rules cache returns the same 100/min token bucket config
steps.action: Rule hasn't changed between requests — same capacity=100, refill≈1.667/s, fail_mode=open. Hard-limit rule (no queue).
steps.codeOrCommand:
snap:= rulesCache.Load
rule:= snap.rules["messaging:api_key:acme_prod"]

steps.title: Lua script returns allowed=0 — bucket empty
steps.action: The script refills by elapsed*rate but tokens are still <1 because the client has been spending them faster than they refill. It writes back the updated {tokens, ts} and returns 0.
steps.codeOrCommand:
-- same script as allow path
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 't','ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local last = tonumber(b[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[1]), tokens + (tonumber(ARGV[3])-last) * tonumber(ARGV[2]))
if tokens < 1 then redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 't', tokens, 'ts', ARGV[3]) return 0
end
--... (not reached)

rl:acme_prod:POST /v1/messages.note: refilled by 0.5s * 1.6667 ≈ 0.83, still below 1 — request denied

steps.decision: allowed=0 → DO NOT call upstream, build 429 response

steps.title: Gateway builds 429 Too Many Requests with all three headers
steps.action: Book p.64 specifies three response headers on deny. retry_after is ceil((1 − tokens) / refill_rate) — how many seconds until at least one token is available.
steps.note: Upstream is never called — that's the whole point. The denied request cost the system one Redis round-trip, not a full backend execution.

steps.title: LB relays the 429
steps.action: Just a return-path TLS wrap. No retry logic at the LB — that's the client's job.

steps.title: Client honors Retry-After, backs off
steps.action: A well-behaved SDK parses X-Ratelimit-Retry-After and waits that long (plus jitter) before retrying. A misbehaving client retries immediately — which, per the client component's bottleneck analysis, is what amplifies load 10× and requires LB-level deny-listing.
steps.codeOrCommand:
if (res.status === 429) { const wait = parseInt(res.headers.get('X-Ratelimit-Retry-After')) * 1000 const jitter = Math.random * 250 await sleep(wait + jitter) // 1.0–1.25s return retryWithBackoff(req)
}

operations.title: Rules worker refreshes the in-memory rules cache
operations.name: Rules worker refreshes the in-memory rules cache
operations.description: The chapter's background loop: a worker pulls the authoritative rule set from disk/config service every 5s and overwrites the in-memory rules cache used by every request.

steps.title: Worker wakes on its 5s jittered ticker
steps.action: Each gateway replica runs an independent rules-worker goroutine. The ticker fires roughly every 5s (±20% jitter) to avoid synchronized poll storms against the config service.
