steps.note: parallel: this loop runs out-of-band from the hot request path. At 1M RPS, the worker's 20 RPS against the config service is invisible.

steps.title: Config service returns rule deltas since the worker's version
steps.action: Delta-only response keyed by version so a no-op poll is ~200 bytes. A product operator bumped the marketing-messaging quota from 5/day to 7/day at T−3s, which lands in this delta.
steps.codeOrCommand:
-- Postgres-backed rule store
SELECT rule_id, domain, descriptor, unit, requests_per_unit, action, version FROM rules WHERE version > 147 ORDER BY version ASC;

steps.title: Worker atomically swaps in the new immutable rule snapshot
steps.action: Worker builds a fresh hashmap off-path (merge of old snapshot + deltas), then CAS-swaps the atomic pointer in one instruction. Readers on the hot path see either the old or the new snapshot — never a half-updated map.
steps.codeOrCommand:
// Go
newSnap:= oldSnap.clone // off-path copy
for _, c:= range delta.changes { newSnap.apply(c) // mutate the copy
}
newSnap.version = delta.to_version // 148
rulesCache.Store(newSnap) // atomic.Value.Store — single instruction
metrics.RulesVersion.Set(float64(newSnap.version))
steps.note: Global propagation time is bounded by the 5s poll; with jitter, all 100 replicas converge within 5–10s. Emergency changes should go via etcd watch / Redis pub/sub (see cfg alternative) for <1s propagation.

operations.title: Rate-limited but soft — enqueue instead of drop
operations.name: Rate-limited but soft — enqueue instead of drop
operations.description: The chapter's 'enqueue rate-limited requests to be processed later' option. Bucket is empty but the request is for a critical flow (e.g., order submission), so the gateway returns 202 Accepted and parks the work on the throttled queue.

steps.title: Client submits an order during a Black Friday surge
steps.action: User clicks Place Order. The endpoint is flagged soft-limit in the rules (critical business flow — dropping is worse than delay). Same api_key as the allow path but now on /v1/orders.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /v1/orders HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_9f2a7b3c
Idempotency-Key: ord_01HW3ZMX8V
Content-Type: application/json {"sku":"widget-42","qty":1,"deadline_sec":30}
steps.note: Idempotency-Key is mandatory on enqueue paths so dequeue dedup works against client retries.

steps.title: LB forwards to a gateway replica
steps.action: Same least-conn routing. The LB doesn't care that this is a soft-limit route — that's a rule-level decision.

steps.title: Gateway authenticates, enters limiter
steps.action: Auth resolves the bearer to api_key=acme_prod. Gateway tags the context with the route so the limiter can find the `/v1/orders` rule — which has action=enqueue, not action=deny.
steps.codeOrCommand:
ctx.principal = auth.verify(req.headers.authorization)
ctx.route = "POST /v1/orders"
ctx.idempotency_key = req.headers['Idempotency-Key']
await rateLimiter.check(ctx)

steps.title: Limiter loads the soft-limit rule and calls Redis
steps.action: Rules cache returns `{capacity: 50, refill: 50/60s, action: enqueue, queue: throttled-orders, deadline_sec_max: 60}`. Middleware still runs the Lua token-bucket check — the difference is what it does when tokens=0.
steps.codeOrCommand:
rule = rulesCache.lookup("orders", "api_key:acme_prod")
// rule.action == "enqueue" (not "deny")
bucket_key = `rl:acme_prod:POST /v1/orders`
result = redis.evalsha(TOKEN_BUCKET_SHA, 1, bucket_key, rule.capacity, rule.refill_rate, now)

steps.title: Token bucket is empty — Lua returns allowed=0
steps.action: Same Lua script as the hard-deny path — Redis doesn't know about the soft/hard distinction; it just reports whether a token was available. The enqueue decision is made by the middleware after reading the result.
steps.codeOrCommand:
-- same token-bucket script as allow/deny paths
if tokens < 1 then redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 't', tokens, 'ts', ARGV[3]) return 0
end
steps.decision: allowed=0 AND rule.action='enqueue' → park the request instead of 429

steps.title: Middleware enqueues the request with a deadline
steps.action: The raw request (headers + body + principal + deadline) is serialized onto the throttled-orders topic. Dequeue workers drain it later, paced to the bucket refill rate, so upstream is never over-driven.
steps.codeOrCommand:
await queue.publish("throttled-orders", { id: req.idempotency_key, // ord_01HW3ZMX8V principal: ctx.principal.api_key, route: ctx.route, body: req.body, enqueued_at: now, deadline_ms: now + 30_000, // 30s from client attempts: 0
})
steps.note: parallel: dequeue workers run asynchronously. They pull at ≤ rule.requests_per_unit per second so draining can't outrun the bucket refill and re-deny itself on EVALSHA at dequeue time.

steps.title: Gateway returns 202 Accepted (not 429)
steps.action: Body includes the idempotency key as a tracking handle. Client can poll GET /v1/orders/:id or (preferably) register a webhook. Rate-limit headers still reflect bucket state so the client can self-pace future calls.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return Response( status: 202, headers: { 'X-Ratelimit-Limit': rule.requests_per_unit, // 50 'X-Ratelimit-Remaining': 0, 'X-Ratelimit-Retry-After': 1, 'Location': `/v1/orders/${req.idempotency_key}` }, body: { id: req.idempotency_key, // ord_01HW3ZMX8V status: 'queued', estimated_process_by: iso(now + queue.depth / rule.refill_rate_per_sec) }
)

steps.title: LB relays the 202
steps.action: Return path — same as allow/deny, just a different status code.

steps.title: Client receives 202, registers a callback
steps.action: SDK sees 202 (not 429, not 200), interprets it as 'accepted for async processing', and wires the response handler to the webhook/poll path. The user sees an order-placed confirmation with 'processing' state — not a failure.
steps.codeOrCommand:
if (res.status === 202) { ui.showOrderPending(res.body.id, res.body.estimated_process_by) // Prefer webhook over polling (see client-component bottleneck #3) awaitWebhook(res.body.id, { timeoutMs: 60_000 })
}

tradeoffs.rationale: Allows configurable bursts, O(1) per check, and tiny state; fixed window allows 2x burst at boundaries and sliding-window-log is O(N) memory.

tradeoffs.chosen: Redis with Lua scripts (vs per-gateway local counters)
tradeoffs.rationale: Gateway replicas must agree on one counter; Lua gives single-RTT atomic check-and-decrement. Local counters would over-admit by a factor of N replicas.
Eventual consistency on rules is fine since rule changes are rare (<100/min); pull avoids config-service outages blocking the hot path.
Most APIs prefer brief over-admission to outright downtime during limiter outage; payment APIs may invert this and fail closed.

tradeoffs.chosen: Per-POP limiter with async delta reconciliation
tradeoffs.rationale: Strong global counters would add cross-region RTT per request; per-POP plus eventual reconciliation accepts a small over-admission window.
